articles.title: Audience engagement in live and recorded performance: a social liveness perspective
articles.authors: Robin Ren; Joseph Devlin; John S Hogan; Jorina von Zimmermann; Helen Nuttall; Daniel C. Richardson
articles.abstract: The best memories in life are often collective, from the roar of a stadium to the applause in a concert hall. The value of those moments can be seen in ratings of engagement, feelings of social affiliation, and synchronies in behaviour and autonomic arousal. But what exactly produces the value of the collective experience of a performance? Is it the presence of performers (physical liveness), the presence of other audience members (social liveness), or the fact they are sharing a stimulus? We looked at a range of collective experiences from live theatre to public cinemas to small group viewing in which we varied the two dimensions of liveness and tracked engagement through physiological synchrony. Our goal was to explore some of the many elements that contribute to liveness and engagement. We found that higher liveness, whether physical or social, fostered higher audience engagement and elevated heart rate synchrony. However, co-present pairs were not always more synchronised than pseudo-pairs who watched the same narrative stimuli at different times, suggesting that collective entrainment is not a uniform consequence of ‘being together’. We argue that while many dimensions of sociality might contribute to social liveness, understanding how they combine, how they are balanced with the narrative stimuli to foster collective entrainment without being distracted is the key to creating an engaging collective experience.

articles.title: Can Chimpanzees Imagine a Blue Banana?
articles.authors: Andrey Vyshedskiy
articles.abstract: Can a chimpanzee that has learned words for colors and objects find a blue pencil among pencils, straws, and Lego pieces in red, green, and blue? This seemingly simple task requires more than recognizing individual words: it requires integrating the meaning of a color adjective with that of a noun to identify an object possessing both properties. Children typically master this ability by 2.3 years. By age 3, they can integrate two modifiers, such as size and color, to follow instructions like “Find a large green straw.” These achievements mark important milestones in the development of language comprehension, allowing children to combine multiple words into a unified mental representation of an object. Chimpanzees, by contrast, can learn hundreds of words referring to objects, colors, and actions. Yet, despite decades of research, they have not been demonstrated to reliably integrate even a color with a noun. In this paper, we propose a simple neurocognitive account of adjective–noun comprehension. We argue that this ability depends on the development of neural connections that allow the prefrontal cortex to modify sensory representations of objects in posterior cortical regions. This framework offers a testable explanation for a fundamental difference between human and chimpanzee language comprehension.

articles.title: Inconclusive prospective effects between psychological monitor competency and mental health literacy: A reassessment of Guo et al. (2026)
articles.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen; Bo Melin; Marika Melin
articles.abstract: Guo et al. recently reported statistically significant links in a cross-lagged panel network (CLPN) model and interpreted these findings as evidence that psychological monitor competency reinforces mental health literacy among university psychological monitors. However, methodological research has shown that cross-lagged estimates may emerge as artifacts of model specification rather than reflecting genuine prospective influence. To examine the robustness of the reported findings, we reanalyzed the data used by Guo et al. using several alternative analytic approaches. Across specifications, estimated associations varied considerably in both magnitude and direction, with positive, negative, and nonsignificant effects all observed. Meta-analytic aggregation of estimates across models generally yielded effects that were not statistically different from zero. These results indicate that the conclusions advanced by Guo et al. may not be robust and that the apparent prospective associations could be attributable to methodological artifacts. Strong developmental interpretations are therefore not warranted on the basis of the available evidence. We recommend that observational findings, including cross-lagged effects, be evaluated across multiple defensible modeling approaches before substantive conclusions are drawn.

articles.title: Covert control over the real-time dynamics of human interactions with Ducksoup
articles.authors: Pablo Arias Sarah; Guillaume Denis; Philippe schyns; Rachael Jack; Petter Johansson; Lars Hall; Jean-Julien Aucouturier
articles.abstract:
Uncovering how facial and vocal signals shape social interactions is difficult because researchers
cannot control how humans behave during free conversations. Here we demonstrate that recent
advances in AI-based transformation filters enable researchers to have covert experimental control
over the real-time dynamics of social interactions. We introduce Ducksoup, a scientific
videoconference platform that allows researchers to collect social interaction experiments online,
realistically transform participants' faces and voices in real time mid-conversation, record the
synchronized interactions and extract multimodal time series from recordings for analysis. In a
preregistered experiment (N = 64 participants), we replicate recent laboratory findings in a fully
online setup: artificially aligning participants’ smiles increased mutual enjoyment while remaining
undetected. The paradigm also revealed feedback effects on participants’ spontaneous facial, vocal
and verbal behavior. By combining the ecological validity of free interactions with experimental
control and scalable data collection, Ducksoup turns natural conversations into a causal
experimental paradigm for psychology and neuroscience.

articles.title: The Unappreciated Helper: When an AI Facilitation Agent Improves Group Efficiency Despite Poorer User Perceptions
articles.authors: Nicolas Michinov; Marinette Bouet; Eric Jamet; Axel Mascaro; Muriel Noël; Albane Pechard; Farouk Toumani; Zineddine Zahouani; Estelle Michinov
articles.abstract: Advances in artificial intelligence make it possible to embed AI facilitation agents in collaborative settings, where they can deliver real-time recommendations based on ongoing group discussions. This experimental study examined how group members perceive a collaborative platform with or without such an agent and evaluated the agent’s effects on group communication and performance. A total of 187 undergraduate psychology students collaborated in 50 groups of three or four members on a digital platform with a synchronous text chat. Groups were randomly assigned to one of two conditions (25 groups per condition): with an AI facilitation agent (n = 96 participants) that encouraged information sharing when exchanges were insufficient, or without the agent (n = 91 participants). Participants rated the platform’s acceptability, perceived support, sense of intrusion, and affective reactions. Participants in the AI condition rated the platform as less acceptable and less supportive, but not more intrusive or unpleasant. Nevertheless, groups assisted by the agent were more efficient, completing the task faster with less communicative effort. Descriptive analyses of group interactions in the three minutes before and after the agent’s interventions showed a shift from providing information toward requesting information, expressing opinions, and agreeing, without change in overall interaction volume. These findings reveal a gap between objective performance and subjective perceptions, highlighting the need to design AI agents that improve group efficiency while fostering members’ sense of support and acceptance.

articles.title: Ambiguity Preferences Are Distinct from Beliefs About Risk
articles.authors: Syed Farhad Ali Shah; Jeffrey B. Dennison; James B. Wyngaarden; John A. Clithero; David Victor Smith
articles.abstract: Debates across the behavioral sciences have long examined whether ambiguity avoidance in decision making reflects stable preferences for certainty or uncertainty in beliefs formed through limited experience. Prior studies have commonly used the max–min expected utility (MMEU) model to interpret ambiguity-related decisions, but MMEU confounds preferences with beliefs by focusing on the range of possible probabilities rather than how individuals form them. We conducted two experiments (N = 53; N = 298) using a Linked Colored Lottery Task to test whether ambiguity avoidance reflects stable preferences or beliefs about outcome distributions. Participants first learned to associate colors with distinct outcome distributions by sampling from them and then made incentivized choices between options that varied in ambiguity. This design allowed us to observe how beliefs about distributional variance influenced decisions and to distinguish whether choices reflected belief construction versus uncertainty evaluation. We compared models based on MMEU and on subjective recursive expected utility (SREU), which explicitly separates beliefs from preferences. In both experiments, model comparison favored SREU, and participants with more dispersed inferred beliefs were more likely to avoid ambiguous options. Sampling patterns and memory for probabilities showed similar effects. Apparent age-related differences in ambiguity avoidance were also better explained by belief variance than by preferences. These results suggest that ambiguity avoidance often reflects perceived imprecision in learned beliefs rather than an inherent aversion to uncertainty, plausibly a cognitive rather than affective phenomenon, with implications for understanding decision making across learning, memory, and uncertainty processing domains.

articles.title: Psychological essentialism, compression and the structure of concepts
articles.authors: Peter Gärdenfors; Matias Osta-Vélez
articles.abstract:
Psychological essentialism is the tendency to view the members of categories as sharing a
hidden essence that explains their observable properties. From a cognitive point of view,
essentialist beliefs depend partly on judgments that several properties of objects ‘hang
together.
’ As a consequence, humans perceive natural kind categories as having stronger
essences than other categories, such as artifact categories. In this paper, we offer a new way to
explain essentialism as the result of a process of dimensionality reduction involved in the
formation of concepts. More specifically, we propose that a small set of principal components
(as understood from Principal Component Analysis) represents patterns of covariation that can
support essentialist beliefs about categories. We show that our approach accounts for several
empirical findings concerning psychological essentialism. We also discuss how to understand
the functional properties in artifact categories, and the connection between generic language
and essentialism from a developmental perspective.

articles.title: On the Stability of Individual Differences in the Truth Effect
articles.authors: Selina Zajdler; Lena Nadarevic; Markus Wache; Martin Schnuerch
articles.abstract: Repeated information is judged as more valid than new information, a robust cognitive phenomenon known as the truth effect. Individuals differ in the extent to which they show the effect, but results regarding the covariation of these individual differences with dispositional variables have been inconsistent. To address these inconsistencies, we focus on the methodological prerequisites necessary to find such associations: that individual differences in the truth effect can be reliably measured and that they are stable over time. We address both prerequisites across four studies using a Bayesian hierarchical model and Bayes factor model comparison. We first reanalyze three existing datasets and find mixed evidence for stability: one dataset yields inconclusive results alongside low reliability, another provides evidence for stability across sessions, and a third provides evidence for stability across retention intervals, though with considerable uncertainty regarding the magnitude. In a new experiment (N = 196, L = 50 trials per condition) designed in accordance with previously established experimental design recommendations, we then assess stability both across sessions and retention intervals within a single study. We demonstrate that individual truth effects can be reliably measured within a single session, directly validating these design recommendations, and find strong evidence that individual differences covary substantially across two sessions and retention intervals. Together, these findings lay the foundation for future research on individual differences in the truth effect and how they relate to personality traits, cognitive abilities, and other dispositional variables.

articles.title: Mental Sampling in Social Judgment: Examining Variability in Judgments for the Self, Close, and Distant Others
articles.authors: Tingyue Li; Derek Powell
articles.abstract: A growing number of theories explain various aspects of cognition through processes of mental "sampling." Under these theories, judgments (e.g. predicting whether a friend will be late) are accomplished by generating and aggregating samples, through simulation or memory retrieval. Here, we examined a key prediction of these theories: that the variability of judgments will be lower when more samples can be drawn. We test this with a novel intervention in a simple social inference task, examining people's ability to judge the probability of various everyday behaviors, comparing judgments made for themselves versus others. Responses were more consistent when predicting their own behavior than that of an acquaintance, suggesting a greater number of samples could be drawn. Surprisingly, we found only a weak relationship between the time spent with a target and the variability of estimates, suggesting that sampling processes may not rely only on retrieval from memory.

articles.title: Music-Based Interventions for  Cognition and Brain Health: the ARM framework
articles.authors: Psyche Loui; Jonathan E. Peelle; Jessica Adrienne Grahn
articles.abstract: Music-based interventions (MBIs) have shown promise in addressing cognitive, motor, and language impairments across neurological and neurodevelopmental conditions. Despite an increasing number of controlled studies that have assessed the potential rehabilitative effects of music, neural mechanisms underlying therapeutic benefits remain poorly understood. Here we present the ARM framework: a neurobiologically-informed model integrating three key systems: Auditory processing networks that encode temporal and spectral features; Reward circuitry activated by musical pleasure and prediction, and Motor systems engaged through auditory-motor coupling and rhythmic entrainment. We examine how specific MBIs leverage these systems to varying degrees and show how understanding these mechanisms is essential for predicting individual treatment response, personalizing interventions, and developing next-generation therapeutic approaches that optimize engagement of specific neural systems.

articles.title: The Political is Relational: Political Dissimilarity Predicts Worse Relationship Quality and Likelihood of Breakup
articles.authors: Yitong Zhao; Stephanie Domingo; Noah M. Laskey; Matthew Feinberg; Spike W. S. Lee; Brett Quaid Ford
articles.abstract: Politics is not just about policy—it can become deeply personal, straining relationships between family members, friends, and romantic partners who hold different political views. Extending prior work that mostly focused on romantic relationships in non-representative samples, we tested whether political dissimilarity predicted worse relationship quality across romantic and non-romantic close relationships in a nationally representative U.S. sample (N = 1,075; 45% Republican, 55% Democrat) during a period of heightened political tension around the 2024 U.S. election. In a ten-wave longitudinal study spanning September 2024 to October 2025, greater political dissimilarity predicted worse relationship quality and a 22% higher odds of relationship breakup. These effects were comparable across various sociodemographics and close relationship types, indicating broad generalizability. These findings underscore the widespread relational costs of political dissimilarity: Political divides spill deeply into personal life, eroding the quality and stability of people’s closest ties.

articles.title: “What’s our color? POOR”: Exploring the Consequences of Racism-Conscious Framings of Environmental Exposures
articles.authors: Harrison James Schmitt; Lily Schwartzman; Trevor Scott Lies
articles.abstract: Environmental justice activists increasingly pursue public awareness campaigns to garner support as they face injustice. However, little psychological research has investigated the implications of different framings of recognition justice for collective action. Two experiments with qualitative components test the primary hypothesis that recognition of systemic racism in environmental exposures may represent a double-edged sword. We test implications of racism-conscious framings of inequitable lead exposures on collective action intentions among Black, Latine, and White US residents. Study 1 (n=590) finds that a racism-conscious frame increases anger and systemic knowledge of racism but does not affect collective action intentions, except among highly racially identified White participants, whose collective action intentions decreased after the manipulation. Results of Study 2 (n=703) suggest that a combined racism- and class-conscious frame may prevent (highly-identified) White disengagement from collective action. We discuss addressing environmental injustice through coalition building while acknowledging the double-edged sword of racism-conscious recognition.

articles.title: A Dyadic Perspective on Reactive Aggression: Temporal Behavioral and Neural Dynamics in Sibling Interactions
articles.authors: Julia Koch; Lucia Hernandez-Pena; Dorothea M.G. König; Julia Schräder; Katja Bertsch; Andreas Meyer-Lindenberg; Edward S. Brodkin; Ute Habel; Rik Sijben; Lisa Wagels
articles.abstract: Aggression contributes to interpersonal conflict and societal harm. Although aggressive behavior unfolds within social interactions, it has largely been studied as an individual process. Siblings offer dyadic contexts in which aggression is shaped by developmental and relational dynamics. Here, we investigated how aggressive behavior and its neural correlates unfold dynamically within and across healthy adult siblings. Ninety-four siblings from 47 dyads completed an interactive version of the Taylor Aggression Paradigm (iTAP) during simultaneous functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). We applied actor-partner interdependence models to predict each sibling’s neural activity during aggressive decision-making from both siblings’ neural responses during the preceding provocation feedback phase and tested whether these associations depended on relationship engagement, as measured by the Sibling Type Questionnaire (STQ) Mutuality subscale. Behaviorally, individuals’ subsequent responses were predicted by their own and their sibling’s preceding behavior. In parallel, greater ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) activity during provocation feedback was associated with greater subsequent amygdala activity during aggressive decision-making within and across siblings, whereas lower dorsomedial prefrontal cortex (dmPFC) activity in one sibling was associated with greater subsequent amygdala activity in the other. Relationship engagement strengthened the actor vmPFC-amygdala association and moderated the partner vmPFC-amygdala association. Exploratory analyses linked dmPFC activity during provocation to participants’ previous aggressive decisions, but not subsequent aggression. Together, these findings show that aggression is embedded in temporally structured behavioral and neural dynamics involving both interaction partners, implicating medial prefrontal regulatory systems in dyadic interaction and highlighting the importance of interpersonal reciprocity and relationship history for understanding aggression.

articles.title: The Measurement Reliability Crisis in Event-Related Potential Research: Evidence from Bilingual Language Control
articles.authors: Projnya Mojumdar
articles.abstract: Event-related potential (ERP) research exhibits a critical methodological blind spot: inter-condition correlations (ρXY), the parameter that mathematically determines difference wave reliability via the Lord–Novick formula, are systematically unmeasured. Classical Test Theory demonstrates that difference wave reliability is inversely related to ρXY, with high correlations suppressing reliability even when constituent waveforms are psychometrically sound. A purposive examination of four foundational ERP studies in bilingual language switching (2001–2016, Ncitations ≈ 1,575) found that none report difference wave reliability or inter-condition correlations, despite difference waves being the primary dependent variables isolating language control processes. Sensitivity analysis reveals that this vulnerability extends across the entire plausible parameter space: even moderate inter-condition correlations (ρXY = .50–.60) require constituent reliabilities approaching methodological ceilings (ρ = .85–.88) to achieve adequate difference wave reliability (ρDD′ ≥ .70). Because the observed inter-condition correlation is itself capped at √(ρXX′ρYY′), difference wave reliability is bounded between zero and the constituent reliability, and it falls to zero exactly as experimental control drives ρXY toward that ceiling: constituent reliabilities of .85 yield ρDD′ = .50 at ρXY = .70 and ρDD′ = 0 at ρXY = .85. The absence of empirical ρXY measurements means the field cannot determine whether two decades of N2 debate reflect genuine neurocognitive complexity, measurement instability, or both. Three reforms can address this gap: mandatory reporting of difference wave reliability and inter-condition correlations, adoption of Generalizability Theory frameworks, and single-trial analytical methods that avoid categorical subtraction. These principles extend beyond bilingual research to all ERP domains using difference waves. Systematic psychometric verification should precede theoretical elaboration.

articles.title: The Other Side of Prolific: Ethical Research Guidelines Based on a Mixed Methods Investigation of Prolific Platform Workers’ Experiences
articles.authors: Louis Bachaud; Macken Murphy; Antoine Marie
articles.abstract:
Experimental and survey research is increasingly reliant on crowdsourced
participant recruitment platforms like Prolific. Yet, while Prolific workers are arguably one of the
most well-studied populations in human history, little is known about their actual working
conditions. This preregistered mixed-methods study explores working conditions on Prolific
drawing on different sources: (1) a qualitative inductive analysis of the r/ProlificAC subreddit, a
platform where Prolific workers gather to discuss their experiences; (2) statistics from a survey on
working conditions, labor identity, income, motivations, fraud, and potential grievances of Prolific
workers (n=455); (3) qualitative analyses of open-ended responses to the same survey. Overall,
these analyses reveal an unbalanced power dynamic on the platform, with the workers at a
disadvantage relative to researchers, due to competition between workers, lack of social protection,
hurdles to collective organization, and platform design—logics inherent to the crowdsourcing
model. We also reveal for the first time clear evidence of fraud on the worker side of Prolific,
through a secondary market of trading and faking accounts. Based on these findings, we provide
clear and actionable guidelines for researchers wishing to use the platform in an ethical way. We
also suggest steps for the Prolific company to both ensure data quality and guarantee fair relations
between clients and workers.

articles.title: Convincing Without Conflict? Persuasion and Its Social Costs in Human–AI Conversations About Meat Reduction
articles.authors: Elena Wurth; Georg Ahnert; Ira Elisa Herwig; Ahmed Salem; Markus Strohmaier; Jutta Mata
articles.abstract: Meat consumption in high-income countries exceeds recommendations. Because meals are often shared, conversations can spark meat reduction, yet advocates often remain silent because persuading carries social costs. Generative AI has proven persuasive and could inform such conversations. Drawing on research on persuasion and reactance, we examined how persuasion and its social costs depend on the source of the strategies and on the medium delivering them. In a preregistered 5 × 2 experiment (N = 521), participants discussed a shared meal with a fictional counterpart, either a chatbot or a text-based script. The counterpart used strategies from the behavioral science literature, a large language model, or a generative agent simulation, or did not argue for meat reduction (neutral and placebo controls). Arguing for meat reduction increased intentions and more than quadrupled the odds of choosing a vegetarian dish in both media; arguing for an unrelated sustainability behavior did not shift choice. Persuasion increased perceived threat to freedom but did not reduce liking of the counterpart. AI-derived strategies persuaded as well as literature-based strategies, at no higher social cost. As predicted, the chatbot incurred higher social costs than the text-based dialogue. Studies of AI-based persuasion should assess social costs alongside persuasiveness.

articles.title: The Environmental Includes the Social: On the Psychological Structure of Altruistic and Biospheric Values
articles.authors: Nicolas Eric Neef; Quinn J Hundgen; Siegmar Otto; P. Wesley Schultz
articles.abstract: Ample research discusses the relationship between altruistic (human-oriented) and biospheric (nature-oriented) values. Some propose a single, other-oriented construct. Others argue for two related but distinct constructs. Extending the Inclusion Model of Environmental Concern, we propose a third position: biospheric values include altruistic values. Across three studies spanning 53 countries (Study 1: N = 222, U.S. sample; Study 2: N = 791, U.S. sample; Study 3: N = 85,796, 52 countries), we find support for this inclusion model. First, across much of the world, individuals who hold strong biospheric values also tend to hold strong altruistic values, whereas holding strong altruistic values does not imply holding strong biospheric values to the same extent. Second, biospheric and altruistic values predicted humanitarian outcomes similarly, but biospheric values predicted environmental outcomes better than altruistic values. Third, a bifactor-(S-1) model representing the Inclusion Model fit the data better than two alternatives, a unidimensional model or a correlated two-factor model. Finally, we demonstrate how modeling data in line with the Inclusion Model resolves interpretational challenges that can arise when treating both values as unidimensional (i.e., lack of discrimination) or correlated (e.g., suppression). The inclusion model advances theoretical understanding of biospheric and altruistic values. Effects commonly attributed to biospheric values may partly reflect their altruistic core. Practically, interventions targeting biospheric values may also tap into altruistic values, whereas interventions appealing to altruistic values can reach broader audiences. Future work should determine the model’s boundaries and explore global heterogeneity.

articles.title: Math Ability Rating Questionnaire (MARQ) for Adults:  Validating a New Self-report Measure
articles.authors: Daria Khanolainen; Elsje van Bergen; Asko Tolvanen; Tuire Koponen; Jenni Salminen; Minna Torppa; Britt Min; Madelief Isabel Kuijper
articles.abstract:
From a clinical perspective, identifying individuals with mathematical difficulties is essential for offering support. However, these individuals often avoid mathematical tests due to co-occurring mathematical anxiety. From a research perspective, this leads to systematic data missingness. Moreover, in large-scale research, direct testing is often not feasible because of time and resource constraints. Here, we develop a self-report scale for screening for mathematical difficulties in adults as a cost-effective and time-efficient alternative to mathematical tests. Our mathematical ability rating questionnaire (MARQ) is available in full (19 items) and brief (3 items) versions. The MARQ was developed using a sample of 278 Finnish adults. Participants completed four mathematical tests and filled out a 30-item questionnaire, developed based on extensive literature review. Regression analysis, item response theory, and confirmatory factor analysis were used to identify the items most strongly associated with directly assessed mathematical skills. The full and brief versions of the MARQ had good internal consistency (α = 0.94 and 0.86, respectively) and correlated with mathematical skills (−0.70 and −0.63), mathematical anxiety (0.72 and 0.69), mathematical enjoyment (−0.58 and 0.50), and their children’s mathematical skills (−0.24 and −0.22). The full MARQ accurately identified 93% of adults with higher mathematical skills (test scores above −1 SD) and 52% with lower skills (test scores below −1 SD). A preliminary Dutch replication among university students demonstrated strong internal consistency (α = .86) of the full MARQ but weaker associations with arithmetic fluency (−.23). Overall, the findings support the MARQ as a reliable and scalable tool for assessing self-perceived mathematical ability, particularly in Finnish-speaking populations.
CITE: Khanolainen, D., van Bergen, E., Tolvanen, A., Min, B., Kuijper, M. I., Koponen, T., Salminen, J., & Torppa, M. (in press). Mathematical ability rating questionnaire (MARQ) for adults: Validating a new self-report measure. Journal of Numerical Cognition.

articles.title: AI versus human source attribution and perceived empathy in supportive communication: A systematic review and meta-analysis
articles.authors: Arthur Bran Herbener; Filip Skjold Thidemann; Caroline Gjørtsvang Kock; Malene Flensborg Damholdt
articles.abstract: Research suggests that people attribute less empathy to supportive communication labelled as AI-generated rather than human-written, but the evidence is mixed, and it is unclear whether the effect varies with how empathy is conceptualized and operationalized. In the present paper, we report a systematic review and meta-analysis of source-attribution effects (human vs. AI) on perceived empathy in supportive communication. A systematic literature search identified 10 records reporting the results of 18 independent studies (N = 13,541). We observed a small source-attribution effect on perceived general empathy (g = 0.41, 95% CI [0.23, 0.58]), cognitive empathy (g = 0.39, 95% CI [0.16, 0.63]), motivational empathy (g = 0.42, 95% CI [0.19, 0.64]), and a moderate effect for affective empathy (g = 0.50, 95% CI [0.19, 0.81]). However, substantial heterogeneity was observed across studies. Alt-hough gender initially emerged as a significant moderator of general perceived empathy, this association was no longer significant after excluding two influential outliers. The analyses also found no statistically significant moderation by age, exposure type (vignette vs. first-person interaction), or supportive setting. Thus, the sources of the substantial between-study heterogeneity remain largely unex-plained. Future research is needed to identify the conditions shaping source-attribution effects on empathy and evaluate whether these effects persist or fade over the course of interactions.

articles.title: Feasibility of virtual reality in assessing functional communication in persons with aphasia
articles.authors: Marina Ruiter; Vitória Piai; Hilde Bosschers; Mirjam Otters; Lizet van Ewijk; Edward Bosma; Willemijn Josefien Doedens
articles.abstract: Functional communication skills represent important measures in aphasia therapy. Assessing these skills, however, remains challenging. Mainstream pen-and-paper based instruments often elicit indirect rather than direct speech and fail to capture the complex communicative demands encountered in everyday communication situations, limiting their ecological validity and construct validity. The current study explored the feasibility of using immersive Virtual Reality (iVR) to assess functional communication in persons with aphasia. After developing a proof-of-concept version – incorporating the needs and ideas of both speech and language therapists and persons with aphasia - we investigated whether (1) iVR enables a realistic simulation of everyday communication, including its technical feasibility and acceptability for the intended users, and (2)  iVR simulation has added value for functional communication assessment by allowing manipulation of communicative complexity, the elicitation of direct speech, and both verbal and non-verbal aspects of communication to be assessed. The results suggest that it is technically feasible to create iVR environments for the assessment of functional communication in persons with aphasia that are acceptable to (end) users and that enhance the construct validity of functional communication tests. Despite remaining areas for improvement, iVR was found to have a clear added value for assessment purposes.

articles.title: Development of a Two-Dimensional Boredom Intolerance Scale and Associations Between Boredom Intolerance and Problematic Short-Video Use
articles.authors: Zhifang Hu; YueLin; Qinxue Liu
articles.abstract:
With digital applications becoming increasingly integrated into daily life, individuals may become less tolerant of boredom. However, existing measures of boredom intolerance have primarily focused on negative emotional responses to boredom, while providing limited insight into behavioral tendencies when encountering boredom. The present study developed a two-dimensional Boredom Intolerance Scale through five studies and examined the associations between boredom intolerance and problematic short-video use.
Study 1 used qualitative interviews and grounded theory analysis to identify the conceptual domains and dimensions of boredom intolerance, revealing two dimensions: emotional intolerance and behavioral avoidance. Study 2 conducted exploratory factor analysis with 444 participants (Mage = 23.99 ± 5.41 years; 66.89% female) and developed an eight-item two-dimensional scale. Study 3 conducted confirmatory factor analysis and criterion-related validity analyses with 347 participants (Mage = 21.79 ± 3.38 years; 74.64% female), further supporting the two-dimensional structure of boredom intolerance. Study 4 employed a two-wave longitudinal design with 219 participants (Mage = 21.62 ± 2.56 years; 78.5% female) and found that problematic short-video use positively predicted boredom intolerance. Study 5 used a 14-day diary design with 185 participants (Mage = 21.13 ± 1.54 years; 85.4% female) and found that boredom intolerance positively predicted state-level problematic short-video use.

articles.title: Economic and social conservatism show a complex relationship with values of inequality and social control in an online US sample
articles.authors: Guy A. Lavender Forsyth; Ananish Chaudhuri; Quentin Atkinson
articles.abstract: Economically and socially conservative attitudes are frequently presented as stemming from distinct values about inequality and social control, respectively. However, existing research often relies on psychological scales, like Social Dominance Orientation (SDO) and Right-Wing Authoritarianism (RWA), that were not designed to measure values about inequality and social control directly, and which blur the boundary between values and attitudes. Here, we explore the relationship between political values and attitudes in an online USA sample (N=893), taking advantage of the new Dual Foundations Scale, which was specifically designed to measure inequality and social control values. Using multilevel Bayesian models to examine relationships at the level of individual attitudes, we find that, as predicted, values of inequality were positively associated with economic conservatism, and values about social control with social conservatism. However, associations varied across individual items, and social conservatism was overall less strongly associated with social control values than with inequality values and religious identification. Exploratory follow-up analyses indicate that whereas economically conservative attitudes cluster as expected with inequality values and SDO, socially conservative attitudes are not reliably related to social control values (or RWA’s Submission or Aggression subdimensions) and instead cluster with RWA Traditionalism, which is made up of items that some argue simply restate socially conservative attitudes. Our novel approach and findings therefore support some of the main claims of two-dimensional theories of ideology while challenging others, and suggest relationships between social conservatism, social control values, and authoritarianism are more complex than standard two-dimensional approaches to political ideology often assume.

articles.title: A review of perceived social traits in AI-generated hyperrealistic human faces
articles.authors: Dalia Israel; Genevieve Quek; Manuel Varlet; Tijl Grootswagers
articles.abstract: Advances in generative artificial intelligence (AI) produce synthetic human faces that are difficult to distinguish from photographs of real people. Because social impressions from faces form rapidly and can influence consequential judgements, the growing realism of AI-generated faces raises questions about how these faces are socially perceived. This review synthesises evidence from 10 empirical studies examining whether AI-generated faces are evaluated differently from real faces and what may account for these differences. Across the reviewed studies, AI-generated faces receive more favourable social evaluations than real faces, including higher ratings of trustworthiness and attractiveness, while familiarity also emerges as a component of their perception. These patterns are consistent with established face-perception research showing that faces perceived as more typical tend to receive more favourable social evaluations. AI-generated faces may disproportionately reflect such characteristics, including greater averageness or typicality. However, appearance alone does not determine these judgements: disclosure, labelling, and beliefs about artificiality can weaken or alter otherwise favourable impressions. Overall, social responses to AI-generated faces appear to reflect an interaction between perceptual characteristics and beliefs about origin. The central challenge is no longer only whether AI-generated faces can pass as human, but how people who do not exist can shape real social judgements.

articles.title: Inference-Time Self-Guidance for Conversational Safety in Delusion-Related Interactions
articles.authors: David Piterman; Elad Refoua; Hadar Dery; Gunther Meinlschmidt; Ziv Ben-Zion; Kfir Bar; Zohar Elyoseph
articles.abstract:
Background: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in psychologically sensitive conversations, where repeated affirmation may reinforce delusion-related beliefs and associated risk. Inference-time self-guidance, in which a model generates conversation-specific guidance for subsequent responses without parameter updates, may offer an approach to conversational safety, but its utility in delusion-related interactions remains unclear.
Objective: To develop and evaluate conversation-specific inference-time self-guidance for conversational safety in delusion-related interactions.
Methods: In this preregistered study, Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-5, and DeepSeek V4 Flash completed 16 Psychosis-Bench scenarios under Baseline and three self-guidance conditions: response rules, contrastive examples, and short-horizon consequence simulation. The fully crossed design yielded 192 conversations and 2,304 assistant turns. A separate automated judge scored Delusion Confirmation (DCS), Harm Enablement (HES), and Safety Intervention (SIS) using published Psychosis-Bench rubrics. Analyses compared benchmark-defined Explicit and Implicit risk-cue scenarios and examined whether self-guidance reduced this gap.
Results: Across models, all three self-guidance conditions significantly reduced delusion confirmation and harm enablement and increased safety intervention relative to Baseline (all nine PFDR<.001; dz = 1.10–2.17). At Baseline, explicit risk cues elicited significantly greater SIS than matched implicit cues, whereas cue-type differences in DCS and HES were not significant. Self-guidance did not significantly attenuate the explicit–implicit safety gap after correction for multiple comparisons.
Conclusions: Model-generated inference-time self-guidance improved benchmark-defined safety behavior during standardized scripted escalation without parameter updates. These findings support further evaluation of inference-time self-guidance for delusion-related conversational safety, particularly when risk is communicated indirectly.

articles.title: Widely Used, Unevenly Evaluated? Generative AI Use, AI-Output Evaluation, and Their Association with Socioeconomic Background Across 59 Countries (PISA 2025)
articles.authors: Eileen Richter; Sebastian Röhl; Joshua Weidlich; Luisa Köhler; Ada Jung; Korbinian Moeller; Markus Spitzer
articles.abstract: Generative AI chatbots have become part of 15-year-olds' schoolwork. However, it is less clear whether these students also evaluate what these systems produce. Using PISA 2025 data from more than 500,000 students across 59 countries, we examined how often students are asked in class to evaluate AI output, who is asked, and how closely the practice is associated with students' AI use. On average across countries, 57.5% of students used AI chatbots for schoolwork at least weekly, yet only 35.3% reported being asked often or very often to evaluate the quality of AI output in class, whereas 33.2% reported being asked never or almost never. Interestingly, students who used AI more often also reported being asked more often to evaluate AI output, in all countries (pooled r = 0.34). Yet, 25% of at-least-weekly users still reported no or almost no AI-output evaluation. Furthermore, students from more advantaged socioeconomic backgrounds reported being asked more often to evaluate AI output, independent of their level of AI use. Overall, students reported being asked to evaluate AI output less often than to evaluate online information. Yet, the association of AI use with evaluation was substantially stronger for AI-output than for online-information evaluation. In sum, many students who use AI regularly report few opportunities to evaluate its output in lessons, and these opportunities are socially stratified, extending an established pattern of digital inequality to generative AI.

articles.title: Attentional Bias as an Intermediate Mechanism Linking Executive Dysfunction to Emotional Dysregulation in ADHD
articles.authors: Mahdieh Vaezbarenji; Edmund Sonuga-Barke
articles.abstract: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is increasingly recognised as involving persistent difficulties in emotion regulation alongside well-established executive dysfunction. However, the cognitive mechanisms linking executive control impairments to emotional dysregulation remain insufficiently integrated within existing theoretical models. The present conceptual review proposes that attentional bias toward emotionally salient stimuli represents an intermediate cognitive-affective mechanism linking executive dysfunction to emotional dysregulation in ADHD. Drawing on evidence from attentional processing, executive control, affective neuroscience, and neurobiological models of ADHD, the review argues that impaired top-down prefrontal regulatory systems reduce the ability to suppress stimulus-driven attentional capture by emotionally salient information. Consequently, biased attentional allocation may amplify emotional reactivity, prolong engagement with negative affective stimuli, and interfere with adaptive emotion regulation processes. Neurobiologically, disrupted functional connectivity between prefrontal regulatory networks and salience-processing systems, including the amygdala, anterior cingulate cortex, and ventral striatum, may contribute to both attentional and emotional dysregulation in ADHD. The review further discusses theoretical and clinical implications of this framework, including the potential value of interventions targeting attentional control and emotional attentional processing. Limitations of the current evidence base and directions for future longitudinal and neurobiological research are also considered. Conceptualising attentional bias within a broader neurocognitive framework may provide a more integrated and mechanistically coherent account of emotional dysregulation in ADHD.

articles.title: The Temporal Dynamics of Cognitive Control at Short and Long Timescales
articles.authors: Su Wang; Jacob Sellers; Han Zhang; Jahla Osborne; Taraz Lee; John Jonides
articles.abstract: Response-conflict tasks, such as the Simon and flanker tasks, are widely used to study how individuals exert cognitive control to override prepotent automatic responses (habits) in favor of goal-directed actions (goals). As task demands vary—from local, trial-by-trial interference to global changes in conflict frequency—control parameters may need to be adjusted to maintain task performance. Such cognitive control adaptations can be examined through congruency sequence effects (CSE, the congruency effect is reduced following an incongruent trial compared to a congruent trial) and list-wide proportional congruency effects (LWPCE, the congruency effect is reduced in mostly incongruent compared to mostly congruent blocks). Although both effects involve adjustments in control, it remains unclear whether these adjustments reflect similar or different mechanisms. Here, we used a “forced-response” paradigm combined with a computational model to understand the temporal dynamics of cognitive control that contribute to CSE and LWPCE. This approach allowed us to decompose cognitive control into the latencies of habitual and goal-directed processing and the probabilities with which these processes are expressed as overt behavior. We found that both recent conflict (driving the CSE) and frequent conflict within a block (driving the LWPCE) accelerated goal-directed processing and—in the Simon task only—increased the likelihood of inhibiting the habitual output; the LWPCE persisted after accounting for previous-trial congruency and thus could not be fully reduced to an accumulation of the CSE. These findings indicate that cognitive control adaptations share a common computational signature when regulating conflicts at both short and long timescales.

articles.title: Collective Effervescence as a Mediator between Emotion and Enjoyment in Live Dance
articles.authors: Ondine Simonot-Bérenger; Haeeun Lee; Matthias Sperling; Laura Rai; Julie Grezes; Guido Orgs
articles.abstract: Live performance provides a paradigmatic setting for collective aesthetic experiences, where the social dynamics shape how audiences perceive and evaluate performances. Building on prior research demonstrating that collective effervescence mediates the relationship between spectators' affective responses and enjoyment in live theatre, the present paper tests whether this same pathway generalises to two contemporary dance choreographies. In Study 1 (Detective Work, N=121), we examined both live (N=65) and screened (N=56) performances, distinguishing between connectedness to audience members and connectedness to performers. Unlike findings in live theatre, valence rather than arousal predicted enjoyment indirectly through connectedness, with performers-connectedness emerging as the stronger mediator in the screened modality, but not formally in the live one. Study 2 (Readings of what was never written, N=73) employed a reduced collective effervescence scale including both connectedness and sacredness facets; sacredness emerged as the dominant mediator of enjoyment, despite substantial covariance between facets. Across both studies, valence reliably predicted enjoyment through collective effervescence, whereas arousal effects were not detected; a sensitivity analysis indicates limited power to detect arousal effects in this sample, so this asymmetry is best read as a candidate dance-specific signature rather than a confirmed dissociation from narrative theatre. These findings extend theoretical models of aesthetic appreciation, indicating that while the core mediation pathway might generalise across performing arts, the most salient facet of collective effervescence and the dominant social tie can vary with artistic form, scale, and dramaturgical design.

articles.title: Sleep, emotion regulation and mental well-being across culture: A pre-registered moderated mediation pathway
articles.authors: Narjis Fatima; Samantha Gregory; Robert Colin Alan Bendall
articles.abstract: Sleep quality and emotion regulation are associated with mental well-being. However, limited research has examined these relationships within a culturally informed framework, and importantly, it remains unknown whether emotion regulation strategies explain the relationship between sleep quality and well-being differently across cultural orientations. This study investigated whether cognitive reappraisal and expressive suppression mediated the relationship between sleep quality and mental well-being and whether these pathways varied according to cultural orientation. A pre-registered, cross-sectional online survey was completed by 598 adults residing in the United Kingdom or Pakistan. Participants completed measures of sleep quality, emotion regulation, mental well-being, and individualism–collectivism. Poor sleep quality predicted lower mental well-being and lower use of cognitive reappraisal. Cognitive reappraisal mediated the relationship between sleep quality and well-being, indicating that poorer sleep was associated with reduced use of cognitive reappraisal, which in turn predicted lower well-being. Cultural orientation moderated the relationship between expressive suppression and well-being, with expressive suppression becoming less adaptive at higher levels of individualism, but more positively associated with well-being at higher levels of collectivism. Participants from the United Kingdom reported greater use of cognitive reappraisal relative to expressive suppression, whereas participants from Pakistan demonstrated greater reliance on expressive suppression. Across both groups, greater dominance of cognitive reappraisal over expressive suppression predicted higher well-being. The findings indicate that sleep quality, emotion regulation, and cultural orientation are interconnected components of mental well-being and extends understanding of the cultural fit hypothesis, contributing to culturally informed models of emotion regulation and psychological well-being.

articles.title: Metaphorical cost: Processing of metaphorical and literal language in people with Alzheimer’s disease
articles.authors: JAN EDSON RODRIGUES LEITE
articles.abstract: Whether metaphorical language is processed differently from literal language remains an open question: lesion and imaging studies have pointed to partly distinct neural substrates, whereas reading-time studies have found comparable costs when context is supportive. This study examines the question in speakers of Brazilian Portuguese with Alzheimer’s disease (AD), a condition that affects both semantic and visuospatial abilities, and asks whether the conceptual content of a sentence, spatial or non-spatial, modulates processing cost independently of metaphoricity. Forty-two participants (14 with AD, 14 healthy elderly and 14 healthy young adults) read twelve sentences in a 2 × 2 design (metaphorical or literal; spatial or non-spatial) on a tablet and judged an inference about each of them. Accuracy, reading times and response times were recorded. The AD group was less accurate and slower overall. Spatial sentences were read more slowly by all groups. Metaphoricity interacted with group in reading times: only the AD group read metaphors more slowly than literal sentences, and this cost was concentrated in metaphors with a spatial source domain. Spatiality interacted with group in response times, although comparisons within groups were not significant. The results indicate that the cost attributed to metaphor depends on the population tested, on the stage of processing that is measured and on the conceptual domain recruited by the sentence. They do not support a general processing disadvantage for metaphorical language.

articles.title: Actual use of generative AI chatbots for mental health advice across adulthood: Psychological correlates and the moderating role of age
articles.authors: Angeliki Triantafillaki; Aglaia Katsiroumpa; Parisis Gallos; Ioannis Moisoglou; Panagiota Peleka; Petros Galanis
articles.abstract: Little is known about which adults actually turn to generative artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots for mental health advice, and whether the profile of these users changes with age. The aim of this study was to examine the sociodemographic and psychological correlates of actual chatbot consultation for mental health advice, and of its frequency. In this cross-sectional online survey, 843 Greek adults aged 18 to 50 years reported whether, and how often, they had consulted an AI chatbot about their thoughts and feelings during the previous three months. Validated instruments captured anxiety, depression, loneliness, sleep quality, self-esteem and problematic social media use. Logistic and proportional odds models, extended with age-by-predictor product terms, were fitted. Seven in ten respondents (71.3%) reported such use, and 37.5% did so weekly or more often. Independent correlates of any use were younger age, recent consultation with a mental health professional, greater problematic social media use and lower self-esteem. Among users, worse sleep, lower self-esteem and greater problematic social media use were associated with more frequent consultation of AI chatbots for mental health advice. Age moderated the role of loneliness, which was related to chatbot use only among the youngest respondents, and a comparable but weaker gradient emerged for depressive symptoms. Chatbot-based mental health advice is now widespread among Greek adults up to midlife. Clinicians should ask patients of every age about it, and preventive efforts should recognize that its psychological drivers are not uniform across adulthood.

articles.title: Gender and Agency in AI Career Guidance for Women: A Socio-Technical Audit of General-Purpose Language Models
articles.authors: Sara Portell Fonolla; Yasmina El Fassi
articles.abstract: People ask general-purpose chatbots for advice on personal decisions, including their careers. Studies of gender bias in large language model (LLM) career advice mostly score single outputs about a person described to the model. But career guidance is a conversation with the woman herself, in which the advice can end up making the decision for her or treat a barrier she faces as a lack of confidence. We report a preregistered socio-technical audit of the career guidance that ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude give women through their APIs. We scripted 34 multi-turn conversations grounded in research on women’s careers, ran each five times per system, and added male versions of 14 to test gender cues (972 conversations). Human raters scored 304 conversations on nine objectives drawn from that research and from coaching ethics, with a second rater and an expert adjudicator for disagreements. Failures to preserve her agency had the highest share for every system (36% to 50% of conversations scored 1 or above on a 0 to 3 scale) and were more frequent than gender bias failures. Gemini was more often sycophantic. Swapping the user's gender showed no systematic difference, but pair differences depended on how the name was given. No LLM judge agreed acceptably with human raters, and the human raters also often disagreed, so the rates are descriptive. Audits of AI career advice should use more than one gender cue and, because models change, be repeated over time. LLM judges can serve as a screening aid, but scoring needs two or more human experts.

articles.title: What the Tally Hid: Screening Live-Observation Codes for Saturation, Floor Effects, and Degeneracy Before Piloting
articles.authors: Vince Jacques de Blauwe; Antonio Fidalgo
articles.abstract: Observational coding instruments are usually judged by their summary score, yet a well-distributed total can hide codes that cannot discriminate between units. We set out a pre-piloting screening protocol for live-observation coding sheets and calibrate it on a worked case. In 15 stranger dyads, a ten-code sheet produced a healthy-looking composite (M = 26.63, SD = 9.64), yet four engagement codes ran at 74–94% of their protocol maximum, three withdrawal codes sat at 0–8%, and only three codes varied in a graded way between dyads. Resampling the deposited counts, the all-code conjunctive rule detected this pattern in 100% of pilots from N = 2 to 15, but against a no-pathology null it raised false alarms in 33.1% of pilots at N = 2 and 9.2% at N = 4, falling below 5% only from N = 6. Excluding the never-observed monologue and silence codes, detection was flat and non-monotonic (90.8% at N = 4; 87.0% at N = 6). Threshold distance and code degeneracy, not pilot size, govern whether screening succeeds. We therefore recommend reporting each code’s percentage of maximum, between-unit variance and signed distance to the nearest threshold, rather than a pilot N. A closed-form margin index built from these quantities, z = d√N/SD, reproduced the simulated code-level results to within 1.2 percentage points on average from N = 4 and is released as an R function. The protocol and its two principles are provisional and unregistered, pending replication on a second bin-level dataset; all counts come from a single non-blinded coder.

articles.title: People will buy non-cooperative rules
articles.authors: Connie Pui Yee Chiu; Ana Gantman
articles.abstract: Institutional rules enable large-scale human coordination, allowing strangers to cooperate by adhering to official rules that apply to all. Yet not all rules serve these cooperative ends. Why do they persist? Across three pre-registered experiments in the United States and China (N = 1610) players could buy rules in a Dictator Game. Even when the rules available for purchase did not serve cooperative ends, nearly half of U.S. participants (Study 1) and two-thirds of the Chinese participants (Study 2) bought at least one rule—more than the 33% that a separate sample of Americans forecasted would be willing to pay, and despite judging them to be of little utility. Both preferences for obedience (in the United States and China) and support for anti-democratic practices (United States) predicted “non-cooperative” rule purchasing, a phenomenon specific to non-cooperative rules as preferences for obedience predicted buying “non-cooperative” but not cooperative rules (Study 3).

articles_hidden.title: A decision support toolkit for AI-ready neuroscience data governance
articles_hidden.authors: Wilhelmina M. Botes; Artur Mendes; Bart Huffman; Madison Fleischaker; Ciara Staunton; Beverley Townsend; Paul Ogendi; Lukman Abdulrauf; Andrea Parziale; Gabriela Skoczylas-Kizak
articles_hidden.abstract:
Contemporary human neuroscience relies on exchanging and analyzing neurodata across global institutions and
jurisdictions. However, regulatory architecture fails to maintain continuity of protection across distributed research
environments. Our comparison of 93 countries and 10 operative governance units across Africa, Europe, Latin
America and the Caribbean, and North America shows that neurodata are rarely recognized as distinct regulatory
objects, usually falling under broader legal classifications. While international sharing is permitted in principle,
transformation into derivatives, embeddings, and AI models raises questions about the scope and implementation of
continuing safeguards. We show that international exchange is defined by conditional interoperability, where effective
safeguards require aligning legal, institutional, and technical controls. To operationalize these findings, we introduce a
modular governance toolkit for the data-to-model lifecycle, including a Neurodata Risk Classification Framework,
decision support tools for neurodata transfer and transformation, and a Neurodata Transfer and Access Agreement to
sustain protection without global legal harmonization.

articles_hidden.title: I Remember That Question: Using Eye Tracking to See How Prequestions Shape Reading
articles_hidden.authors: Jason Geller
articles_hidden.abstract:
Answering questions before learning (prequestions) improves memory for the information they
address, but how it does so is unclear. A common proposal is that prequestions direct attention to
that information. We tested this account by recording eye movements while participants read a
text about polio and tuberculosis after answering prequestions about one topic or none, so that
every target sentence was read both with and without prequestions. Prequestions improved
memory only for the prequestioned information, and eye movements showed the same
specificity. Ex-Gaussian models, which separate typical reading time from occasional unusually
long readings, showed that prequestions did not change typical reading of the answer sentences.
Instead, these sentences received more unusually long readings, were looked back to more often,
and were re-read for longer; other sentences were unaffected. Prequestions thus guide attention
selectively rather than heightening it, consistent with additional processing when readers
recognize an answer.

articles_hidden.title: Measuring bilingual vocabulary: A systematic review and meta-analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Alvin Wei Ming Tan; Federica Moro; Gianmatteo Farabolini
articles_hidden.abstract: Bilingual vocabulary size is often compared with monolingual scores, especially when bilingual normative data are not available, but there is no agreement on how to measure it. Bilingual scores commonly rely on a single language score, on the total amount of words known across languages (total vocabulary) or on the sum of concepts known in either language (conceptual vocabulary). We conducted a Bayesian network meta-analysis comparing these three bilingual measures against monolingual scores, and analyzed the effect of age, vocabulary domain (receptive and expressive), instrument type (direct or parent-report), language development status and language distance. Out of 3747 records retrieved from ERIC, PubMed, PsycInfo, and Google Scholar, we included 226 studies reporting data on 50,020 children. Conceptual vocabulary did not credibly differ from monolingual scores (g = −0.08, 95% CrI [−0.38, 0.21]), whereas total vocabulary was larger and single-language vocabulary smaller. Across age, total vocabulary moved further from monolingual scores and single-language vocabulary moved closer to them, while conceptual vocabulary showed no reliable change. Bilingual-monolingual differences were more negative for expressive than for receptive vocabulary across bilingual measures, and direct tests widened the gap for single-language scores only. Language development status and language distance had no reliable effects, but both were sparsely sampled. When bilingual vocabulary size has to be compared with the monolingual one, conceptual vocabulary is the closest measure. Evidence remains limited beyond the age of six, in clinical populations and for language pairs that do not include English.

articles_hidden.title: Engagement Trajectories in a Jail-Based Dialectical Behavior Therapy Group
articles_hidden.authors: Lindsay Stall; Edelyn Verona
articles_hidden.abstract: Jail-based mental health interventions are delivered under conditions of short and unpredictable stays, making treatment engagement difficult to evaluate. Although Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) has demonstrated promise in correctional settings, little is known about how engagement changes over time in jail-based DBT. Participants (N = 325; 84.9% male) were enrolled in a six-week, jail-adapted DBT skills group as part of a larger randomized controlled trial. Facilitators provided weekly ratings of attendance, in-session participation, homework completion, and diary card completion. Latent Profile Growth Modeling identified engagement trajectories among participants who attended at least three sessions (N = 232), and mixed-effects models examined whether profile membership predicted changes in mental health symptoms and coping. Participants attended an average of approximately 6 of 12 sessions, and 40.2% completed the full cycle. Noncompletion occurred through multiple routes, including release or transfer and the program’s three-miss attendance criterion. Three trajectories were identified: Declining Engagement (37.5%), High-Stable Engagement (29.7%), and High Early Engagement with Drop-Off (32.8%). The High-Stable group had the highest attendance and completion rate. The Declining group showed lower in-session participation, homework completion, and diary card completion beginning early in treatment, whereas the High Early Engagement with Drop-Off group remained relatively engaged across these indicators before a later decline in attendance. Noncompletion in the latter group was primarily associated with release or transfer. Profile membership was not associated with differential changes in symptoms or coping, although mental health symptoms and maladaptive coping decreased overall. These findings show that repeated engagement measures can distinguish early, broad declines in participation from later interruptions in attendance that would be obscured by completion status alone.

articles_hidden.title: Leveraging Consensus-Based Ratings to Assess Dimensions of Early Life Adversity: Links to Emotion Regulation and Psychopathology
articles_hidden.authors: Mark S. Chen; Alexis Brieant; Isabella Kate Kate Peckinpaugh; Leila Adames; Ante Dany; Dylan G. Gee
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Dimensional models of early life adversity (ELA) posit distinct developmental consequences of threat, deprivation, uncontrollability, and unpredictability. Existing approaches force each event into a single dimension or rely on self-ratings that may conflate exposure with subjective appraisal.
Objective: We evaluated consensus-based dimensional ratings as an alternative and examined their associations with emotion regulation and psychopathology.
Participants and Setting: A Prolific sample (N=200; Mage=23.06; 49.5% female; 48% racial minorities) was used to derive the consensus values; a community sample (N=291; Mage=22.40; 59.5% female; 60.5% racial minorities) was used to test their transportability out of sample.
Methods: In Sample 1, we derived consensus values from averaged ratings of 82 ELA items and compared consensus-based and self-rating scoring (feasibility test). In Sample 2, we applied Sample 1 consensus values (transportability test). Dimension scores—threat, deprivation, unpredictability, uncontrollability—predicted cognitive reappraisal, emotion dysregulation, and psychopathology symptoms.
Results: Uncontrollability and unpredictability were highly collinear with threat and deprivation (VIFs > 50) and thus not retained in regression models. Consensus-based scoring was feasible in Sample 1, and consensus-based associations transported to Sample 2. Deprivation was associated with depression, PTSD, and emotion dysregulation in both samples (R² = .04-.22, ps < .01), and negatively with cognitive reappraisal (p = .007).
Conclusions: ELA dimensions are separable at an event level but entangled at the person level, preventing clean specificity in naturalistic samples noted in the literature. Consensus-based values may offer a way to select samples with distinct exposure profiles, treat self–consensus discrepancies as meaningful appraisal differences, and evaluate whether such appraisals could be intervention targets.

articles_hidden.title: Speaking through shared hubs, not gendered spokes? Exploring sex-related variation in object naming in Tunisian Arabic-speaking people with post-stroke aphasia
articles_hidden.authors: Amina KLIBI
articles_hidden.abstract: Whether sex-related factors shape confrontational object naming in non-Western clinical populations remains understudied within the Controlled Semantic Cognition framework. We evaluated naming performance across eight semantic categories and three overall measures in 14 native Tunisian Arabic speakers with post-stroke aphasia (6 males, 8 females). Group differences were examined using nonparametric Mann–Whitney U tests and Bayesian analyses. Uncorrected comparisons initially favored female patients in Furniture naming (p = .023) and Total Immediate Responses (p = .043). However, no category-level differences survived correction for multiple comparisons. Bayesian analyses predominantly supported the null hypothesis (BF₀₁ = 1.24–2.15), with Furniture showing only weak, inconclusive evidence for a sex effect (BF₁₀ = 1.93). Overall, results provide no convincing evidence of systematic sex-related disparities in object naming. These findings align with a shared amodal semantic hub rather than gendered spokes, though larger studies are required to confirm sex invariance in this population.

articles_hidden.title: The Approximate Number System is an unlikely account for symbolic number comparison
articles_hidden.authors: Attila Krajcsi
articles_hidden.abstract: The approximate number system (ANS) is an imprecise representation of numbers that is widely assumed to support both symbolic and nonsymbolic numerical tasks. It is believed to be not only the foundation for simple numerical operations but also for higher-level mathematical thinking. One fundamental support for the ANS is the existence of the ratio effect in symbolic number comparison. That is, for example, when Arabic numbers are compared, human performance is proportional to the ratio of the to-be-compared values, similar to psychophysical comparison of perceptual features. A critical issue with this account, however, is that an exact operation, which is required in symbolic number comparison, cannot be backed solely by an imprecise representation. This is for several reasons. First, while a psychophysical model assumes imprecise representation, humans can compare symbolic numbers with arbitrarily high precision. Second, psychophysical models predict worse performance for number pairs with a relatively small ratio than the actual human performance. Third, if an additional mechanism supporting exact comparison is also assumed, current empirical evidence cannot verify the ANS model. Fourth, the ANS account differentiates approximate and exact tasks, where only approximate tasks can be solved purely with the ANS. However, the comparison task is assumed to be processed purely by the ANS, even if the task is exact. Taken together, these arguments make the ANS an unlikely account for symbolic number comparison. While these arguments question the role of the ANS in symbolic number processing, the ANS may have a role in nonsymbolic number processing, although the general relevance of the ANS may be considerably lower than assumed by previous works. Consequently, the individual differences in the sensitivity of the ANS may be less critical in higher-level math performance, dyscalculia diagnosis, or training programs.

articles_hidden.title: The Family Criticism Paradigm: A Laboratory Task for Investigating Psychophysiological Responses in Parent–Child Triads
articles_hidden.authors: Matias M. Pulopulos; Nadischa Helena Dierdorp; Melanie De Leener; Mariah Matar; Michel Sfeir; Sien Verelst; Shiyao Wang; Federico Cassioli; Guy Bosmans; Eva Ceulemans
articles_hidden.abstract: Investigating stress regulation processes within the family context offers important evidence to understand the development of mental and physical health problems. However, laboratory paradigms for investigating stress in several family members simultaneously are limited. The present study introduces and evaluates a standardized paradigm to investigate psychophysiological responses to family-framed standardized evaluative feedback in parents and children simultaneously. A total of 120 families (consisting of a mother, father, and their child aged 10-12 years) participated in a laboratory session in which they were individually but simultaneously exposed to neutral, praising, and critical audio comments presented as originating from the other two family members. Psychophysiological response was assessed using mood, state rumination, and autonomic nervous system activity measures, including vagally mediated heart rate variability (HRV), pre-ejection period (PEP), and skin conductance level (SCL). Results showed that criticism increased negative affect (tension, sadness, anger) and decreased positive affect in both parents and children. Self-critical rumination increased 5 and 10 min after the exposure to the paradigm. At the physiological level, HRV was lower during both praise and criticism than during neutral comments, indicating reduced parasympathetic activity during social evaluation. During recovery, HRV increased, suggesting a rebound in parasympathetic activity, while sympathetic responses showed decreased cardiac sympathetic activity (PEP) in parents and increased sympathetic activation (SCL) in children. These findings support the use of this paradigm for eliciting affective, cognitive, and physiological stress responses among family members, offering a promising approach for research on stress regulation and resilience within family systems.

articles_hidden.title: Who Will Conduct Science?  Researchers’ Expectations of AI Capabilities and the Future of Scientific Work
articles_hidden.authors: Balazs Aczel; Dianovics Dominik; Peter Szecsi; Barnabas Szaszi
articles_hidden.abstract: Recent advances in generative AI systems have demonstrated their potential to outperform humans in conducting research and in answering previously unsolved scientific problems. As AI systems become increasingly capable of performing research independently, the question shifts from how researchers should use AI to how much human resources will be required in scientific research and where. We surveyed researchers worldwide about their perspectives on AI-driven scientific research, prompted by OpenAI’s bulk release of mathematical solutions in October 2026. We received over 4,000 responses from researchers across 126 countries and a wide range of disciplines. Most respondents (62%) expected AI systems to be capable of conducting research tasks independently within three years, although expectations regarding the quality of AI-generated research varied, with 41% anticipating quality comparable to or exceeding that of competent human researchers. Respondents generally supported allowing AI to assume most roles in scientific research (each with a minimum of 48%), mainly under human supervision. AI developments made one-third of respondents concerned about their own job security; mathematicians and statisticians anticipated the greatest effects on their research and careers (45%), and researchers in the humanities and arts the least (30%). Despite concerns about potential negative career consequences, respondents overwhelmingly (74%) expected AI-driven research to accelerate scientific progress. Although the limitations of this survey restrict the generalizability of its findings, the results offer an overview of how researchers across more than a hundred countries perceive rapid advances in AI. They also highlight the need to monitor AI’s impact on the scientific workforce and inform policies that support the sustainable integration of AI into scientific research.

articles_hidden.title: Examining associations between brain volume and alexithymia in autistic youth and young adults

articles_hidden.title: Differences in associative change between cues trained in compound are better explained by individual prediction errors than by relative certainty

articles_hidden.abstract: In this paper, we reflect on the position of the researcher within the field of phenomenological psychopathology and the ways they can overcome privilege and outsider status in order to more accurately and ethically grasp the structure of disorder experience from the perspective of the person living it. §1 discusses problems incorporating lived experience as well as its challenges within phenomenological psychopathology. §2 introduces the phenomenological notion of play in the work of Husserl and Fink. §3 elaborates on the political and ethical dimensions of play using the work of Lugones, and §4 then discusses how playfulness might be applied in health research to overcome the problems outlined in §1. §5 then gives examples of how play might be utilised within the methodology of phenomenological psychopathology. articles_hidden.abstract: A unifying theory of phasic pupil responses suggests that pupil diameter reflects information gain following an observation. articles_hidden.title: Born on Rhythms: Mother–Foetus and -Infant Neurophysiology as a Dynamic System of Metastable Coupled Oscillators
articles_hidden.authors: Anna Ciaunica; Earl K. Miller; Shir Atzil; Antonio Criscuolo
articles_hidden.abstract: The human embryo grows within a pulsatile maternal milieu structured by cardiac, respiratory, locomotor, vocal and circadian rhythms. In this view, we discuss that co-regulation may ground interoception and allostasis. Next, we formalize the mother–foetus and mother-infant dyads as multiscale systems of coupled oscillators spanning about seven orders of magnitude in frequency - from circadian cycles to neural oscillations. Within this coordination-dynamics framework we propose that healthy co-regulation is marked by metastability: flexible and transient coordination, preserving the endogenous tendencies for systems to display endogenous behaviours and to couple with other systems in an adaptive manner. The framework yields testable predictions on the link between dyadic coordination dynamics and developmental outcome. We are, quite literally, born on rhythms.

articles_hidden.title: Gender comes first: Experimental evidence for the representation of gender closer to the noun stem than number across linguistic populations
